strengths: The paper addresses a useful question for researchers in program representation learning: whether source code and generated comments available during pretraining can improve an encoder used on lower-level code alone. The frozen source/comment encoder and learned interpolation provide a plausible approach.

The reported results are promising across several tasks. Function-name classification accuracy improves from 29.41 to 33.41 over RoBERTa, and summarization BLEU-4 improves from 32.43 to 34.36 over GraphCodeBERT. Component ablations and an additional CodeT5 experiment provide useful initial evidence.

The architecture diagram and pseudocode communicate the overall pipeline. Dataset statistics, several training settings, and an archival data/code link provide a useful foundation for reproducibility.
weaknesses: Necessary: Reconcile the POJ-104 task definition. Section 2.3 describes supervised classification with cross-entropy, whereas Section 3.2 and Table 2 specify non-overlapping sets of 64 training, 16 development, and 24 test classes. An ordinary classifier cannot learn the held-out class labels through the stated training procedure. If the experiment actually evaluates retrieval, specify its objective, candidate sets, ranking procedure, and definitions of MAP, MAR, and MAF1. This ambiguity affects both the main results and most ablations.

Necessary: Align the binary-analysis claims with the evaluated inputs. Section 3.1 uses compiler-generated LLVM IR, and Figures 7–8 retain informative function, global, and type names. Name stripping is explicitly described only for function-name recovery. These experiments do not establish performance on stripped executable binaries, and the footnote claiming executable binaries and lifted representations are trivially interchangeable is inaccurate. Either narrow the claims to the evaluated LLVM IR setting or provide evidence using representations recovered from the claimed binary setting.

Necessary: Clarify evaluation independence. Section 3.2 says summarization and translation are evaluated on the validation set, while Section 4.3 describes test-set evaluation. Clearly distinguish pretraining partitions from downstream training, model-selection, and final evaluation partitions. Document duplicate and overlap checks, including between AnghaBench and the GitHub-derived function-name corpus. The manuscript does not establish leakage, but it also does not provide enough information to assess this risk.

Necessary: Strengthen attribution of improvements to interpolation. PCL receives 10 pretraining epochs, while the complete model receives 30 or 70, depending on the task. Section 5.1 asserts convergence of PCL without supporting learning curves. A matched-budget continuation control and separate linear/nonlinear ablations would substantiate the claimed contributions of these components. Repeated runs or suitable uncertainty estimates are also needed to assess robustness, particularly for the smaller improvements.

Necessary: Qualify the conclusions about human-written comments. Table 7 reports a striking MAF1 decrease from 38.19 to 3.06, but the human-comment extraction procedure, function alignment, retained sample counts, and handling of missing or truncated comments are insufficiently described. Length distributions alone do not establish the proposed explanations involving verbosity, implementation details, or stylistic variation. Validate the comparison on matched data and investigate the collapse, or restrict the conclusion to this particular preprocessing and training configuration.

Necessary: Distinguish lexical generation performance from semantic correctness. BLEU, GLEU, ROUGE, and exact match do not establish functional equivalence of reconstructed source or factual accuracy of summaries. Summarization references appear to come from CodeT5; their provenance and quality need clarification. In Figure 7, 'Unloads a mutex' and GraphCodeBERT's 'Unloads the mutex' are semantically equivalent despite the surrounding claim of competing models failing. Retaining the semantic-consistency and comprehension claims requires appropriate independent assessment, such as execution checks or evaluated human judgments; otherwise, narrow the conclusions to reference-based text metrics.

Necessary: Resolve methodological and numerical inconsistencies. Figure 3 concatenates interpolation inputs, whereas Equations 8 and 10 add them; the treatment of gradients through the targets in Equation 5 is unspecified. Give the exact encoder, generation-decoder, and interpolation configurations. Section 5.1 also labels relative percentage decreases as percentage-point decreases: Table 7 shows MAF1 drops of 0.79, 2.85, and 6.97 points, not 2.07, 7.46, and 18.25 points.

Optional: Comparisons with additional binary-specific encoders, sensitivity to compiler optimizations, and analysis of learned interpolation weights would broaden practical usefulness. These extensions are not prerequisites if the core evaluation is clarified and the claims are appropriately scoped.
